readings.c1s1:
¶
'''bedaggle''' (bẹ̄-dag′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''daggle.'' Cf. ''bedag.''] To soil, as clothes, by trailing the ends in the mud, or spattering them with dirty water. ''J. Richardson'', Notes on Milton.

'''bed-ale†''' (bed′āl), ''n.'' Ale brewed for a confinement or a christening.

'''bedare†''' (bẹ̄-dãr′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dare''<sup>1</sup>.] To dare; defy.
{{smaller block|<poem>The eagle . . . is emboldened
With eyes intentive to ''bedare'' the sun.</poem>
{{right|''Peele'', David and Bethsabe.}}}}

'''bedark†''' (bẹ̄-därk′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''bederken''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dark'', ''v.''] To darken.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whan the blacke winter night . . .
''Bederked'' hath the water stronde,
Al prively they gone to londe.</poem>
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., i. 81.}}}}

'''bedarken''' (bẹ̄-där′kn), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''darken.''] To cover with darkness; darken; obscure.

'''bedarkened''' (bẹ̄-där′knd), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Obscured. —'''2.''' Figuratively, existing in mental or moral darkness; sunk in ignorance: as, “this ''bedarkened'' race,” ''Southey''.

'''bedash''' (bẹ̄-dash′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dash.''] To wet by throwing water or other liquid upon; bespatter with water or mud: as, “trees ''bedash’d'' with rain,” ''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 2.
{{smaller block|<poem>So terribly ''bedash’d'' . . . that you would swear
He were lighted from a horse-race.</poem>
{{right|''Middleton'', Anything for a Quiet Life, i. 1.}}}}

'''bedaub''' (bẹ̄-dâb′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''daub.''] To daub over; besmear; soil.
{{smaller block|''Bedaub'' fair designs with a foul varnish.
{{right|''Barrow'', Works, III. xv.}}}}
readings.c1s2:
¶
'''Bedawi''' (bed′a̤-wē), ''n.''; pl. ''Bedawin'' (-wēn). See ''Bedouin'', 1.

'''bedazzle''' (bẹ̄-daz′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dazzle.''] To dazzle by too strong a light; blind or render incapable of seeing clearly by excess of light.
{{smaller block|<poem>My mistaking eyes
That have been so ''bedazzled'' with the sun,
That everything I look on seemeth green.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iv. 5.}}
Sunrise threw a golden beam into the study and laid it right across the minister’s ''bedazzled'' eyes.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, xx.}}}}

'''bedazzlingly''' (bẹ̄-daz′ling-li), ''adv.'' So as to bedazzle.

'''bed-board†''' (bed′bōrd), ''n.'' The head-board or foot-board of a bedstead.

'''bed-bolt''' (bed′bōlt), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', a horizontal bolt passing through both the brackets of a gun-carriage on which the forward end of the stool-bed rests.

'''bedbug''' (bed′bug), ''n.'' The ''Cimex lectularius'' or ''Acanthia lectularia,'' infesting beds. See ''bug''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bed-chair''' (bed′chãr), ''n.'' An adjustable frame designed to enable invalids to sit up in bed. Also called ''chair-bed.''

'''bedchamber''' (bed′chām″bėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''bedchaumbre'' (= MHG. ''bettekammere''); < ''bed''<sup>1</sup> + ''chamber.''] An apartment or chamber intended or appropriated for a bed, or for sleep and repose.—{{smaller|'''Lords of the bedchamber''', officers of the British royal household under the groom of the stole. They are twelve in number, and wait a week each in turn. The groom of the stole does not take his turn of duty, but attends the king on all state occasions. There are thirteen grooms of the bedchamber, who wait likewise}}
readings.c1s3:
in turn. {{smaller|In the case of a queen regnant these posts are occupied by women, called ''ladies of the bedchamber''. In either case they are generally held by persons of the highest nobility.}}

'''bed-clip''' (bed′klip), ''n.'' In ''coach-building'', a band of iron designed to secure the wooden bed of the vehicle to the spring or to the axle.

'''bedclothes''' (bed′klōᴛ̵ʜz), ''n. pl.'' The coverings used on beds; sheets, blankets, quilts, etc., collectively.

'''bed-cover''' (bed′kuv″ėr), ''n.'' A bedquilt or bedspread.

'''bedded''' (bed′ed), ''p. a.'' [Pp. of ''bed''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' Provided with a bed.—'''2.''' Laid in a bed; embedded.—'''3.''' Existing in beds, layers, or strata; stratified, or included between stratified masses of rock. {{smaller|Chiefly used in combination, as thin-''bedded'', heavy-''bedded'', etc. Masses of igneous rock formed by successive overflows of molten material are often said to be ''bedded'', but not ordinarily ''stratified''.}}

'''4.''' Growing in or transplanted into beds, as plants.
{{smaller block|<poem>Dost sit and hearken
The dreary melody of ''bedded'' reeds
In desolate places.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Endymion, i. 239.}}}}

'''bedder''' (bed′ėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who puts to bed.—'''2.''' One who makes beds (mattresses); an upholsterer. [Local, Eng.]—'''3.''' A bed-stone; specifically, the nether stone of an oil-mill. ''Phillips'' (1706). Also ''bedetter''.—'''4.''' A bedding-plant (which see).

'''bedding''' (bed′ing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''bedding'', < AS. ''bedding'' (for *''beddung'') = G. ''bettung''; < ''bed''<sup>1</sup> +
readings.c2s1:
''-ing''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' The act of placing in a bed; a putting to bed, especially of a newly married couple. See ''bed'', ''v. t.'', 4.
{{smaller block|A circumstantial description of the wedding, ''bedding'', and throwing the stocking.
{{right|''Scott'', Nigel, xxxvii.}}}}
'''2.''' A bed and its furniture; the materials of a bed, whether for man or beast.
{{smaller block|<poem>Pray God he have not kept such open house,
That he hath sold my hangings, and my ''bedding!''</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, v. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''geol.'', as used by most geologists, the exact equivalent of ''stratification'', or occurrence in strata or beds. See ''bed'', ''bedded'', and ''lamination''.—'''4.''' In ''building'', a foundation or bottom layer of any kind.—'''5.''' The seat in which a steam-boiler rests.

¶
'''bedding-molding''' (bed′ing-mōl″ding), ''n.'' Same as ''bed-molding''.

'''bedding-plant''' (bed′ing-plant), ''n.'' An ornamental flowering plant or foliage-plant suited by habit for growing in beds or masses, and to produce a desired effect, generally of color, by combination with other plants.

'''bedding-stone''' (bed′ing-stōn), ''n.'' In ''bricklaying'', a straight piece of marble applied to the rubbed side of the brick to prove whether the surface is straight or not.

'''beddy''' (bed′i), ''a.'' Bold; forward. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>But if my puppies once were ready,
They’l be baith clever, keen, and ''beddy''.</poem>
{{right|''Watson’s Collection'', I. 70.}}}}

'''bede'''<sup>1</sup>†, ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''bead''.
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''bede<sup>2</sup>''' (bēd), ''n.'' [Etym. unknown.] In ''English mining'', a peculiar kind of pickax.

'''bedead†''' (bẹ̄-ded′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dead.''] To deaden.
{{smaller block|Others that are ''bedeaded'' and stupefied as to their morals.
{{right|''Hallywell'', Melampronœa, p. 1.}}}}

'''bedeafen''' (bẹ̄-def′n), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''deafen.''] To render deaf.

'''bedeck''' (bẹ̄-dek′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''deck.''] To deck out; adorn; grace: as, “''bedecking'' ornaments,” ''Shak.'', L. L. L., ii. 1; “''bedecked'', ornate, and gay,” ''Milton'', S. A., l. 712.
{{smaller block|<poem>Such wonderful and priceless gifts as these,
Fit to ''bedeck'' the limbs of goddesses!</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 245.}}}}

'''bedeen''' (bẹ̄-dēn′), ''adv.'' [North. E. and Sc., < ME. ''bedene'', ''beden'', ''bidene'', ''biden''; of uncertain origin; appar. < ''bid-'', which seems to be an unexplained substitute for ''bi'', E. ''by'', prep. (less prob. a corruption of ''mid'', with, or of ''with''), + ''ene'', < AS. ''ǣne'', once, at once, < ''ān'', one: see ''once'', ''one'', and cf. ''anon'', of somewhat similar formation. ''Bedeen'' is often a mere expletive.] '''1†.''' In a body; together: as, all ''bedeen''.—'''2†.''' In order; one after another.—'''3.''' Forthwith; straightway.—'''4.''' Anon; by and by.
{{smaller block|Read on our Bibles, pray ''bedeen.''
{{right|''Blackwood’s Mag.'', XXVIII. 738.}}}}

'''bedegar, bedeguar''' (bed′ẹ̄-gär), ''n.'' [< F. ''bédegar'', ''bédeguar'', ult. < Ar. Pers. ''bādāwar'', a kind of white thorn or this-

''ward'', rose.] A spongy excrescence or gall, sometimes termed sweetbrier-sponge, or robin-redbreast’s pincushion, found on various species of roses, especially the sweetbrier, produced by several insects, as
[[FIGURE]]

''Rhodites rosæ'' and ''R. bicolor'', as the result of puncture and the deposit of their eggs, and containing their larvæ: once supposed to have medicinal properties.

¶
'''bedehouse''', ''n.'' See ''beadhouse''.

'''bedel, bedell''' (bē′dl, bē-del′), ''n.'' [< LL. ''bedellus'': see ''beadle''.] In the medieval universities, a servant of a “nation” or faculty (each of which companies elected two, an upper and a lower, termed the ''esquire bedel'' and the ''yeoman bedel'', terms showing the classes from which they were chosen), whose duties were to apportion the
readings.c2s4: “schools” or lecture-rooms and the chapters of the colleges and halls, to cry the days and hours of the lectures, to publish and carry out the decrees of the company, to march before the rector, dean, or proctor with a silver mace on occasions of ceremony, etc. See ''beadle''.—'''Grand bedel''', {{smaller|the upper bedel of the faculty of theology.}}
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''bedelve†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''bedelven'', < AS. ''bedelfan'', < ''be-'', about, + ''delfan'', dig: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''delve.''] '''1.''' To dig round or about.—'''2.''' To bury in the earth.
{{smaller block|A man dalf the erthe . . . and fond there a gobet of golde ''bydolven.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, v. prose 1.}}}}

'''bedeman''', ''n.'' See ''beadsman.''

'''beden''' (bē′den), ''n.'' [< Ar. ''baden.''] A kind of ibex.

'''bedene†''', ''adv.'' See ''bedeen.''

'''bederoll†''', ''n.'' See ''bead-roll.''

'''bedesman†''', ''n.'' See ''beadsman.''

'''bedetter†''', ''n.'' Same as ''bedder'', 3, of which it appears to be a corruption.

'''bedevil''' (bē-dev′l), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bedeviled'' or ''bedevilled'', ppr. ''bedeviling'' or ''bedevilling.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''devil.''] '''1.''' To treat with diabolical violence or abuse.
{{smaller block|''Bedevilled'' and used worse than St. Bartholomew.
{{right|''Sterne'', Sentimental Journey, I. 34.}}}}
'''2.''' To possess with or as with a devil.
{{smaller block|One age, he is hagridden, bewitched; the next, priestridden, befooled; in all ages, ''bedevilled.''
{{right|''Carlyle'', Sartor Resartus, iii. 3.}}}}
'''3.''' To “play the devil with”; transform or confuse as if by the aid or agency of evil spirits; confound; muddle; corrupt; spoil.
{{smaller block|So ''bedevil'' a bottle of Geisenhèim . . . you wouldn’t know it from the greenest Tokay.
{{right|''Disraeli'', Vivian Grey, vi.}}}}
'''4.''' To bewilder with worry; torment; bother; confuse.—'''5.''' To make a devil or devils of; bring into the condition of a devil: as, to ''bedevil'' mankind.
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''bedevilment''' (bẹ̄-dev′l-ment), ''n.'' [< ''bedevil'' + ''-ment.''] The act of bedeviling, or the state of being bedeviled; especially, a state of bewildering or vexatious disorder or confusion.

{{smaller block|The lawyers have twisted it into such a state of ''bedevilment'' that the original merits of the case have long disappeared.
{{right|''Dickens'', Bleak House, viii.}}}}

'''bedew''' (bẹ̄-dū′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''bedewen'', ''bedeawen'' (= MHG. ''betouwen'', G. ''bethauen''); < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dew.''] To moisten with or as with dew; moisten in a gentle manner with any liquid.

{{smaller block|The most precious tears are those with which heaven ''bedews'' the unburied head of a soldier.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, xxi.}}}}

'''bedewer''' (bẹ̄-dū′ėr), ''n.'' One who or that which bedews.

'''bedewy†''' (bẹ̄-dū′i), ''a.'' [Erroneously formed from ''bedew'', ''v.''; prop. ''dewy'', < ''dew'', ''n.''] Moist with dew.

{{smaller block|<poem>Dark night from her ''bedewy'' wings
Drops sleepy silence to the eyes of all.</poem>
{{right|''A. Brewer'' (?), Lingua, v. 16.}}}}

'''bedfast''' (bed′fȧst), ''a.'' [< ''bed''<sup>1</sup> + ''fast.''] Confined to bed; bedridden.

{{smaller block|My old woman is ''bedfast.''
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Sylvia’s Lovers, ii.}}}}

'''bedfellow''' (bed′fel″ō), ''n.'' [< ME. ''bedfelow'', ''-felawe;'' < ''bed''<sup>1</sup> + ''fellow.''] One who shares a bed with another.

{{smaller block|Misery acquaints a man with strange ''bedfellows.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 2.}}}}

'''bedfere†''' (bed′fēr), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also, erroneously, ''bedphere'', < ME. ''bedfere'', ''bedifere'', < ''bed'' + ''fere'', companion: see ''fere''<sup>1</sup>.] A bed-

'''bedehouse''', ''n.'' See ''beadhouse''.

'''bedel, bedell''' (bē′dl, bē-del′), ''n.''   [< LL. ''bedellus'': see ''beadle''.]   In the medieval universities, a servant of a “nation” or faculty (each of which companies elected two, an upper and a lower, termed the ''esquire bedel'' and the ''yeoman bedel'', terms showing the classes from which they were chosen), whose duties were to apportion the “schools” or lecture-rooms and the chapters of the colleges and halls, to cry the days and hours of the lectures, to publish and carry out the decrees of the company, to march before the rector, dean, or proctor with a silver mace on occasions of ceremony, etc. See ''beadle''.—'''Grand bedel''', {{smaller|the upper bedel of the faculty of theology.}}

'''bedelve†''', ''v. t.''   [ME. ''bedelven'', < AS. ''bedelfan'', < ''be-'', about, + ''delfan'', dig: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''delve.'']   '''1.''' To dig round or about.—'''2.''' To bury in the earth.
{{smaller block|A man dalf the erthe . . . and fond there a gobet of golde ''bydolven.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, v. prose 1.}}}}

'''bedeman''', ''n.'' See ''beadsman.''

'''beden''' (bē′den), ''n.''   [< Ar. ''baden.'']   A kind of ibex.

'''bedene†''', ''adv.'' See ''bedeen.''

'''bederoll†''', ''n.'' See ''bead-roll.''

'''bedesman†''', ''n.'' See ''beadsman.''

'''bedetter†''', ''n.'' Same as ''bedder'', 3, of which it appears to be a corruption.

'''bedevil''' (bē-dev′l), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bedeviled'' or ''bedevilled'', ppr. ''bedeviling'' or ''bedevilling.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''devil.'']   '''1.''' To treat with diabolical violence or abuse.
{{smaller block|''Bedevilled'' and used worse than St. Bartholomew.
{{right|''Sterne'', Sentimental Journey, I. 34.}}}}
'''2.''' To possess with or as with a devil.
{{smaller block|One age, he is hagridden, bewitched; the next, priestridden, befooled; in all ages, ''bedevilled.''
{{right|''Carlyle'', Sartor Resartus, iii. 3.}}}}
'''3.''' To “play the devil with”; transform or confuse as if by the aid or agency of evil spirits; confound; muddle; corrupt; spoil.
{{smaller block|So ''bedevil'' a bottle of Geisenhèim . . . you wouldn’t know it from the greenest Tokay.
{{right|''Disraeli'', Vivian Grey, vi.}}}}
'''4.''' To bewilder with worry; torment; bother; confuse.—'''5.''' To make a devil or devils of; bring into the condition of a devil: as, to ''bedevil'' mankind.

'''bedevilment''' (bẹ̄-dev′l-ment), ''n.''   [< ''bedevil'' + ''-ment.'']   The act of bedeviling, or the state of being bedeviled; especially, a state of bewildering or vexatious disorder or confusion.

{{smaller block|The lawyers have twisted it into such a state of ''bedevilment'' that the original merits of the case have long disappeared.
{{right|''Dickens'', Bleak House, viii.}}}}

'''bedew''' (bẹ̄-dū′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bedewen'', ''bedeawen'' (= MHG. ''betouwen'', G. ''bethauen''); < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dew.'']   To moisten with or as with dew; moisten in a gentle manner with any liquid.

{{smaller block|The most precious tears are those with which heaven ''bedews'' the unburied head of a soldier.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, xxi.}}}}

'''bedewer''' (bẹ̄-dū′ėr), ''n.'' One who or that which bedews.

'''bedewy†''' (bẹ̄-dū′i), ''a.''   [Erroneously formed from ''bedew'', ''v.''; prop. ''dewy'', < ''dew'', ''n.'']   Moist with dew.

<poem>Dark night from her ''bedewy'' wings
Drops sleepy silence to the eyes of all.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''A. Brewer'' (?), Lingua, v. 16.}}}}

'''bedfast''' (bed′fȧst), ''a.''   [< ''bed''<sup>1</sup> + ''fast.'']   Confined to bed; bedridden.

{{smaller block|My old woman is ''bedfast.''
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Sylvia’s Lovers, ii.}}}}

'''bedfellow''' (bed′fel″ō), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bedfelow'', ''-felawe;'' < ''bed''<sup>1</sup> + ''fellow.'']   One who shares a bed with another.

{{smaller block|Misery acquaints a man with strange ''bedfellows.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 2.}}}}

'''bedfere†''' (bed′fēr), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also, erroneously, ''bedphere'', < ME. ''bedfere'', ''bedifere'', < ''bed'' + ''fere'', companion: see ''fere''<sup>1</sup>.]   A bedfellow.

{{smaller block|Her that I mean to choose for my ''bed-phere.''
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Epicœne, ii. 3.}}}}

'''bed-frame''' (bed′frām), ''n.'' The frame of a bed; a bedstead.

'''bed-gown''' (bed′goun), ''n.'' '''1.''' A night-gown or night-dress.—'''2.''' A kind of jacket like a dressing-sack, usually of printed calico, worn in Scotland by women of the working-class, generally together with a drugget or colored flannel petticoat. Also called ''short-gown.''

{{smaller block|She had wooden shoes, a short red petticoat, a printed cotton ''bed-gown''; her face was broad, her physiognomy eminently stupid.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', The Professor, vii.}}}}

'''bed-hangings''' (bed′hang″ingz), ''n. pl.'' The valance and curtains of a bed.

'''bediamonded''' (bē-dī′a-mo̤n-ded), ''a.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''diamond'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Covered or ornamented with diamonds.

{{smaller block|Astarte’s ''bediamonded'' crescent.
{{right|''Poe'', Ulalume, ii. 21.}}}}

'''bedight''' (bē-dīt′), ''v. t.''; generally or always in pret. and pp. ''bedight'' or ''bedighted.'' [ME., only in pp. ''bediht, bydyght''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dight.''] To array; equip; dress; trick out; bedeck; invest. [Archaic and poetical.]

{{smaller block|A troope of men the most in armes ''bedight.''
{{right|''Mir. for Mags.'', p. 270.}}}}
{{smaller block|His head and beard with sout were ill ''bedight.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. vii. 3.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
